title: Three Silver
subtitle: The Legend of Nine
teaser: The Hollow Hand of Ostrel bought him off the canal steps for three silver and made him the finest killer it ever trained. Then it sent him into the wrong house.

sections.heading: I. Three Silver
paragraphs: He does not remember his name. He remembers the steps.

Saint Orra’s Stairs ran down into the Long Canal of Ostrel, eleven stone steps furred with weed. The children with nowhere else to go slept on the dry ones under the bridge, packed together for warmth. He was four. He had a sack for a blanket and a crust he was saving.
One night a hand came down on his shoulder.
He had not heard footsteps. He had not heard a boat. There was only the hand, warm and dry, and an old man’s soft voice above him in the dark.
“You never heard me,” it said, pleased. “Good. That’s the first lesson.”

A ferrywoman waited at the bottom of the steps with her lantern shuttered. He watched three silver coins pass from the old man’s hand to hers. Then he was under a tarpaulin in the bottom of her boat, and nobody on Saint Orra’s Stairs ever looked for him again.

The Hollow Hand of Ostrel was older than the city’s charter. It was called hollow because it never held anything it could be caught with: no sign, no door, no names. Its knives had killed two doges and more merchants than anyone had counted. Five masters ruled it, called the Fingers, and the eldest, who had founded it, was called the Thumb.
It was the Thumb who had come down Saint Orra’s Stairs. He told the boy that names were for people who expected to be called. The boy was the ninth child bought that winter, so he was Nine.

sections.heading: II. The Game
paragraphs: The Hand kept its children in an old granary below the waterline, where daylight never reached. That was deliberate. On the first night, they held him down and put the drops in his eyes.

The drops were squid ink and something worse, and they burned like vinegar in a cut. Children screamed for three days. Some went blind, and were sold on to the beggar-masters of the port. The others woke seeing in the dark like cats, and for the rest of their lives their eyes shone in it like little red coals. So the first thing they learned was to look at the floor.

Then they learned everything else. Knives. Poisons. Locks. The weight of a sleeping man, and how it changes when he wakes. The black powder that blinds a room for the space of a breath, and how to be somewhere else when it clears.
And every night, they played the game.

A master would come into the children’s loft in the dark and lay a brass coin on someone’s chest. In the morning, if you woke with the coin on you and did not know how it got there, you went without bread. If you caught the master’s wrist, you kept the coin. The masters called it You Never Heard Me, and for years they won every night.
When Nine was eleven, he turned it around.

One morning the Long Finger, who had killed a doge in his bath, woke with a brass coin on his chest. He had not heard a thing. The next morning it was the Ring Finger. The morning after that, there was a coin on the pillow of the Thumb himself.
Any other child would have been drowned for it. Instead the Thumb came down to the loft and studied him the way a smith studies a blade that has come out of the quench without a crack.
“You are the best I have ever made,” he said. “Do you know what that means?”
Nine knew. It meant the most expensive work, and the worst.
By sixteen he had done forty-one. He did not keep count. The Hand did, in a ledger, and charged accordingly.

sections.heading: III. The Merchant’s House
paragraphs: The forty-second was the household of Ilario Castelvo, a salt merchant who had stood up in the doge’s council and said the Hollow Hand was real.
“All of them,” the Thumb said. “Ostrel needs reminding what happens to men who talk.”
Nine went in over the roof at the second bell. The merchant died in his sleep. So did the two hired swords on the stairs. Nobody heard a thing.
The last door on the top floor was a nursery.

There was one small bed. He crossed the room the way he had crossed a hundred rooms, and as he stood over it with the knife held low, the child opened its eyes. It was about four years old. It did not scream. It looked up at the two red coals in the dark and said, in the clear, interested voice of the very small:
“I heard you.”
No one had heard him in twelve years.
He stood there a long time. Then he put the knife away, wrapped the child in its blanket, and went out of the window.

He carried it across the rooftops and left it asleep in the foundling hatch of the Convent of the Narrows. Not on the canal steps. Never there. He did not learn its name, and he never went back. Both were on purpose. The Hand found people through the things they cared about. He made sure there was nothing to find.
In the morning, the merchant’s widow and six servants woke up alive, and the Hand knew by breakfast.
They expected him to run. They sent knives to the gates, the quays and the mountain road. Nobody watched the granary. Nobody had ever been fool enough to go back.
He went back.

The Fingers sat at their long table under a single lamp, waiting for word that he was dead. Nine crossed the room behind them. Nobody heard him. He laid a brass coin on the table in front of the Long Finger, and when the Long Finger looked down at it, Nine cut his throat.
Then he threw the lamp.

The granary was full of rope and oil and grain dust, and it went up like a struck match. He went out through the smoke and barred the water door behind him. Three of the Fingers burned at their own table.
Only three. The Ring Finger was away in the south, selling knives. And the Thumb had not come down that night at all.

sections.heading: IV. The Fingers
paragraphs: He spent the next six years taking the Hand apart with everything it had taught him.

The Ring Finger was the Hand’s merchant. He rented its knives to anyone who could pay, and no one alive knew his face. So Nine hired him. Through three brokers in three cities, he offered the richest contract the Hand had ever seen, on a rogue with red eyes who called himself Nine. It was too much money to trust to a go-between, so the Ring Finger came to meet the client himself, in a wine cellar in the southern port, with four bodyguards.
The client was already sitting in the dark behind him.
“You took the job,” Nine said. “So you’ve been paid.”

The Ring Finger carried a book in his coat: every knife the Hand still had out in the world, and where. Nine worked through it for five years. A poisoner in the passes. A brother and sister who killed for a lake lord. Two cells on the northern coast, grown from children who had slept in the loft beside him. He knew their numbers. He gave each of them one chance: put the Hand’s knife down for good. Two took it. He has not had to visit them since. The rest did not, and he did not miss.

The Thumb was the last, and he had never left Ostrel. He was not even hiding. He had a tall house on the Canal of Lanterns, a new name, and a charity house for the children of the canal steps. The doge had given him a medal for it.
Nine went in over the roof at the second bell.

The old man was awake at his desk, writing by one candle. Nine stood behind him a long time, close enough to read the page. Then he reached past the old man’s shoulder and laid a brass coin beside the candle.
The Thumb looked at it. He set down his pen. He did not turn around.
“I wondered which of you it would be,” he said softly. “I hoped it would be you.”
“You never heard me,” Nine said.
“No,” the Thumb agreed. “I made you well.”
Then it was done.
The book on the desk was the Hand’s oldest ledger: fifty years of children, in the same small, neat hand. Nine found his own near the middle.
Nine. Saint Orra’s Stairs. Three silver. Name not recorded.

The charity house had a cellar with no windows. There were eleven children in it, already learning to look at the floor. He sent them up into the street. Then he burned the house to the waterline, ledger and all, and walked away along the Canal of Lanterns while the bells rang for fire.

sections.heading: V. The Unseen
paragraphs: The Hand is dead. It is not finished.

It sold knives for fifty years, and not all of them were written down. There are students of its students, and men in Ostrel who would like to start it again. Each of them knows the same thing: nobody rebuilds the Hand while Nine is alive.
So he does the one thing the Hand taught him never to do. He lets himself be seen.

He fights in the duelling rings, in the open, under the lamps, in the Hand’s own cloak, black with a teal sheen like night water, scorched to rags in the granary fire. His hood stays up and his red eyes burn inside it, where anyone in the trade will know them. Every bout is a message to whatever is left: Nine is alive, and the Hand is not. Come and fix it.

They come. Some in the crowd, some in the ring, some in the alley afterwards. None of them has ever seen him fight from the front. There is a breath of black smoke, and he is not where your blade went. Then he is behind you, in the place the Hand taught him to live, and both knives are in before you hear a thing.

Every purse he wins goes back to Ostrel, to the ferrywomen of the canal steps. The Hand used to pay them three silver a child. He pays four, to row every child on the steps somewhere the Hand never shopped, before anyone with a soft voice and a full purse comes down the stairs. He does not know their names. He does not want to.

He does not think it squares anything. Forty-one lines in a burned ledger do not square. But the ferrywomen have not lost a child off Saint Orra’s Stairs since he started paying, and that is the only count he keeps.

If you were ever one of the Hand, or you are thinking of buying what it sold, you already know where to find him. Come to the rings. Bring as many knives as you like. Watch for the red in the hood. It won’t help. One night, in the crowd or the alley or your own locked room, a hand will come down on your shoulder, and a quiet voice behind you will tell you the first lesson.
